title: Kinds of jobs
sub: IJob, IJobParallelFor, IJobFor, transforms and Entities jobs — which to pick and why
cards/0/title: IJob: one task on one thread
cards/0/body:
There are several job types, and “which one would you pick” shows whether you understand how work is split between threads.

IJob has one Execute() method that runs entirely on a single worker thread. It runs in parallel only with the main thread and with other jobs; the work itself is not split.

It fits work that does not cut into independent pieces: sorting, a sum, building a data structure, a step that depends on the previous result.
cards/1/body:
IJobParallelFor calls Execute(int index) for every index from 0 up to the given length. When scheduling you pass the length and the batch size — the innerloopBatchCount parameter, usually called batchSize: that is how many iterations a worker grabs at a time. The workers take batches, and an idle worker steals batches from busy ones (work stealing). That is why the order of iterations is not guaranteed.

The safety rule: in Execute(index) you write only to element [index]. In the Editor the safety system stops a write to someone else’s index with an exception — that is how it guards against races between batches.

For light per-element work batchSize is usually 32–128, for very heavy work it can go down to 1. Details are in unit 2, and the profiler always has the last word.
cards/2/q: An IJobParallelFor over 10,000 elements with batchSize 64. What is true?
cards/2/options/0: Iterations run in batches of 64 on different worker threads, and the order of batches is not guaranteed
cards/2/options/2: Iterations run strictly in order from 0 to 9999
cards/2/options/3: Each iteration runs on its own thread
cards/2/explain: Execute is called 10,000 times — once per index. Workers grab 64 iterations at a time and steal batches from each other, so the order between batches is undefined. Hence the rule: every iteration is independent and writes only to its own index.
cards/2/wrong/1: 64 is the batch size, not the number of calls. Execute is called for every index.
cards/2/wrong/2: There is an order only inside one batch on one thread, not between batches.
cards/2/wrong/3: There are as many threads as the Job System has workers, not as many as there are iterations.
cards/3/title: IJobFor: one job, three ways to run it
cards/3/body:
IJobFor (since Unity 2019.3) looks like IJobParallelFor — the same Execute(int index) — but how it runs is decided at the call site:

— Run(length) — right away, on the main thread, in order;
— Schedule(length, dependsOn) — on one worker thread, in order;
— ScheduleParallel(length, batchSize, dependsOn) — in batches on several worker threads, like IJobParallelFor.

dependsOn is the JobHandle of a job that must finish first; default means no dependencies. It is convenient: one struct, and you switch the mode with one line — Run for debugging, Schedule when the data is small or order matters, ScheduleParallel for big arrays.

The trap: Schedule on an IJobFor is not parallel.
cards/4/q: Match the call with where the work runs.
cards/4/pairs/0/1: One whole Execute() on a worker thread
cards/4/pairs/1/1: Right away on the main thread, in order
cards/4/pairs/2/1: Execute(i) for every i on one worker thread
cards/4/pairs/3/1: Batches of 64 on several worker threads
cards/5/body:
A job cannot touch GameObject or Transform — they are managed main-thread objects. Transforms get an exception: a TransformAccessArray holds a list of transforms, and an IJobParallelForTransform gets access to position, rotation and scale in Execute(int index, TransformAccess transform).

An important detail: Schedule(transforms) gives read and write access but parallelizes only separate hierarchies — transforms with a shared root are always processed on the same thread. A thousand bullets under one container object is effectively one thread. Keep such objects at the scene root.

If you only need to read, there is ScheduleReadOnly(transforms, batchSize) (since 2020.2): it reads all transforms in parallel, whatever the hierarchy; check invalid entries with transform.isValid. A transform job has no plain Run — only RunReadOnly. Like native containers, a TransformAccessArray is freed with Dispose().
cards/6/q: What is true about IJobParallelForTransform? Pick all that apply.
cards/6/options/0: With Schedule, transforms that share a root are processed on one thread
cards/6/options/1: ScheduleReadOnly reads transforms in parallel regardless of the hierarchy
cards/6/options/2: In Execute you can call GetComponent<Rigidbody>() on the transform
cards/6/options/3: With Schedule, a thousand objects under one parent spread over all cores
cards/6/options/4: A transform job has RunReadOnly but no plain Run
cards/6/explain: The read-write Schedule parallelizes only separate roots, so objects under one parent run on one thread. ScheduleReadOnly lifts that limit for reading. TransformAccess gives you position, rotation, scale and matrices, not the GameObject: there are no components inside a job.
cards/7/task: Rewrite DistanceJob from IJob to IJobParallelFor: Execute(int index) computes one distance and writes only to distances[index], with no loop inside. In ScheduleDistances schedule it with Schedule(positions.Length, 64).
cards/7/checks/0/label: DistanceJob is an IJobParallelFor struct with [BurstCompile]
cards/7/checks/2/label: Execute writes to distances at its own index
cards/7/checks/3/label: There is no for loop in Execute
cards/7/checks/4/label: Schedule gets the array length and a batchSize
cards/7/explain: The loop is gone: the scheduler took over its role, calling Execute for every index and handing batches of 64 to the worker threads. Each iteration is independent and writes only to its own element, so the safety system is happy and there are no races. For work this light per element, 64 is a reasonable starting batch.
cards/8/body:
The Collections package adds specialised types: IJobParallelForDefer — when the length is unknown at scheduling time (for example, it is the length of a NativeList that an earlier job fills); IJobParallelForBatch — Execute(startIndex, count) receives a whole batch; IJobFilter — selecting indices.

Entities 1.x has jobs of its own. IJobEntity: you write an Execute whose parameters are components (ref to write, in to read), and the source generator turns it into a pass over every matching entity; the struct must be partial. IJobChunk is a level lower: Execute is called per chunk, and you fetch the component arrays yourself. You pick it when you need full control over how a chunk is walked. More in unit 4.
cards/9/q: Interviewer: “10,000 bullets are GameObjects, and each has to move every frame. Which job do you use?”
cards/9/options/0: IJobParallelForTransform with a TransformAccessArray, keeping the bullets at the scene root rather than under one parent
cards/9/options/1: IJobParallelFor that accesses a Transform[] array inside
cards/9/options/2: An IJob that moves all bullets in a loop
cards/9/options/3: IJobFor with Schedule — it is parallel
cards/9/explain: Transforms are touched from a job only through TransformAccessArray and IJobParallelForTransform. If all bullets sit under one parent, the read-write Schedule runs them on one thread — that is why the hierarchy is kept flat.
cards/9/wrong/1: Transform[] is an array of managed objects; you cannot pass it to a job.
cards/9/wrong/2: One thread for everything means no parallelism, and Transform is not available in an IJob anyway.
cards/9/wrong/3: Schedule on an IJobFor runs everything on one worker thread; ScheduleParallel is the parallel one. And Transform is not available there either.
cards/10/q: Fill in the blanks: a parallel job whose run mode is picked at the call site.
cards/10/explain: IJob has no Execute(int). The index in Execute is always an int. A call with a length, a batchSize and a dependency is ScheduleParallel: Schedule on an IJobFor takes no batchSize and runs everything on one thread.
